newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS - Korean note default dents IPC's regional bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Korean note default dents IPC's regional bid.

text.p: Singapore computer firm IPC Corp's hopes of becoming an Asian regional player suffered a blow with news of financial trouble at its Korean unit, analysts said on Monday.
They said news of IPC Corporation (Korea) Ltd's default on promissory notes last week in Korea raised concerns about the company's financial controls.

"The financial impact (on IPC) is not very big as it is limited to a subsidiary. But as the company is trying to be a regional player, implications are bigger as it suggests financial control is very weak," said Patrick Yau, analyst at Schroders Securities.
IPC Corp (Korea) defaulted on 570 million won (US$657,000) of promissory notes, an official at Korea First Bank said.
Timothy Wong, research manager at Vickers Ballas, also said he was concerned about IPC's level of financial control especially in foreign operations.
"This is always the problem the further away you go. All kinds of stuff could go wrong," he said.
IPC said in a statement on Friday it had not been able to find the chief executive officer of IPC Corp (Korea).
Patrick Ngiam, chairman of IPC, told Reuters he did not see the Korean event as poor financial control or a potential setback to becoming a regional player.
"I disagree with this. The South Korean situation is an isolated one," he said in a written statement.
Ngiam said the company had sent a team to investigate the matter in South Korea.
Another analyst at a Singapore broking house said IPC already had a string of problems with its foreign operations.
"This whole phenomenon could be endemic. It has had problems with one market, then another, then another," he said.
IPC closed both its Australian and U.S. operations last year to cut losses and concentrate on Asian market.

"It is trying to get back into Asian market and finding the competition already there. Why is the Korean subsidiary short of cash? It could be the way they have been marketing or cutting their prices," the analyst at the local broking house said.
One of IPC's Korean shareholders, Samick Musical Instruments Co Ltd, which holds a three percent stake in the company, defaulted on 2.7 billion won in notes in October.
On how IPC would account for its Korean exposure, which the company pointed at S$45.5 million (US$32.5 million), Ngiam said it was too early to decide.
Wong of Vickers Ballas said IPC could account for the write-off as an extraordinary loss which would not hurt its net profit.
Vickers has retained its profit forecast of S$9.7 million for IPC for the full year ending December 1997, Wong said, adding 1996 forecast of S$11 million net remained unchanged.
Analysts said even if the Korean unit was wound down, the group would only be slightly dented.
"It would impact in terms of the sales contribution. And if it decides to withdraw from the Korean market totally, there could be inventory write-offs," the analyst at the local broking house said.
Other analysts said how the exposure affects 1996 and 1997 results depended on the company's accounting practices. ($1 = S$1.4 = 867 won)
